history.content: Небольшой Python API выполняет фоновые задания и расписания. Нужны повторы при ошибке. Redis, Valkey, RabbitMQ и Kubernetes запрещены. Есть SQLite; один Python-разработчик. Цель — выпускать функции быстрее, без своей системы очередей.

Поэтому список рекомендаций пуст: это пробел доказательств и состава подборки, а не вывод, что подходящего ПО нет.

Карточки относятся к замороженному каталогу от 2026-09-01 и имеют статус `reference_only`. Переданные host observations от 2026-10-11 — отдельные датированные чтения первичных источников. Я использую их как временные доказательства для ответа; они не обновляют каталог и не означают сохранение результата в `state.json` или offline HTML.

| Вариант | Что подтверждено переданными источниками | Что препятствует выбору |
|---|---|---|
| BullMQ, ID `162494199` | Описание упоминает несколько языков, включая Python, и Redis либо PostgreSQL. [Репозиторий](https://github.com/taskforcesh/bullmq). | Конфигурация с Redis запрещена. | River, ID `716228772` | Фоновые задания на Go; карточка связывает проект с PostgreSQL. [Репозиторий](https://github.com/riverqueue/river). | Для небольшого Python API это вводит другой язык и новую БД. Оснований считать такой переход полезнее сохранения Python нет. |

| Trigger.dev, ID `572570113` | Платформа workflows с основным языком TypeScript. Облачное размещение нельзя считать обходом запретов без выяснения их области действия. |
| Temporal Python SDK, ID `451613653` | Python SDK; карточка указывает durable execution и orchestration. [Репозиторий](https://github.com/temporalio/sdk-python). | Это наиболее близкий по языку объект для проверки, но карточка не подтверждает весь требуемый набор функций, серверную архитектуру и допустимую конфигурацию хранения. Однако карточка и разрешённый ID этого проекта не переданы, поэтому я не включаю его в рекомендации или предлагаемый стек.

**Целевая архитектура для проверки** — сохранить Python API, бизнес-логику и существующую SQLite; добавить один подтверждённо совместимый механизм заданий и отдельный процесс выполнения. Если изменение бизнес-данных и постановка задания должны происходить вместе, команда должна проверить атомарность или предусмотреть восстановление после разрыва между ними. Повтор задания также требует идемпотентной бизнес-операции: наличие retries не доказывает однократность внешнего эффекта.

Предполагаемая продуктовая польза — выпускать новые фоновые функции через общий механизм выполнения, расписаний и повторов. Это может уменьшить объём собственной инфраструктурной логики, но измеренной экономии нет. Команда всё равно отвечает за обработчики, классификацию ошибок, предел попыток, статусы для пользователя, контроль зависших заданий и восстановление.

Основные факторы сложности: версия Python, модель запуска API, постоянство диска, конкуренция записей SQLite, число процессов, длительность заданий, поведение расписаний после простоя и безопасность повторных побочных эффектов. Если нужны несколько хостов или высокая доступность, предпочтение простой локальной схеме может измениться. Возможность отдельного worker не запрещена текущим Brief, но фактическое размещение неизвестно.

**Первая проверка: условно 4–8 инженерных часов**, один Python-разработчик, 8 часов на инженерный день — 0,5–1 рабочий день при полной загрузке. Это плановая оценка проверки, не срок полного внедрения и не выполненная работа. Сначала проверить для Temporal Python SDK документацию выбранной версии: необходимые расписания и повторы, все обязательные компоненты, совместимость Python и отсутствие запрещённых зависимостей. Если обнаружится конфликт, остановить этот вариант. Если конфигурация допустима и среда доступна, проверить одно искусственно падающее задание, предел повторов, один запуск по расписанию и поведение после перезапуска процесса; зафиксировать потерю заданий или дублирование бизнес-эффекта как критерии отказа. Внешнее ожидание доступа или подготовки сервиса в эти часы не входит.

Полная оценка внедрения сейчас **неизвестна**: нет подтверждённого допустимого решения и данных о размещении. Для сравнения одинакового объёма готовый компонент должен покрыть сохранение заданий, расписания, повторы и восстановление после сбоя; к нему добавятся интеграция, эксплуатация и обновления зависимостей. Собственная реализация должна покрыть те же функции, включая конкурентный захват заданий и восстановление незавершённых попыток, а затем поддерживать эти механизмы. Сохранение текущего компонента может оказаться дешевле, если он уже обеспечивает этот объём; текущая реализация не описана. Утверждать преимущество повторного использования по времени или стоимости пока нельзя.

Решающий вопрос для следующего выбора: **API работает на одном хосте с постоянным локальным диском или на нескольких экземплярах / с непостоянной файловой системой?** Ответ определит, допустима ли локальная архитектура и какой объём интеграции сравнивать с собственной разработкой.

history.content: A small Python API needs background jobs, schedules and retries. Redis, Valkey, RabbitMQ and Kubernetes are forbidden. SQLite is available; one Python engineer. We want to ship features sooner without building a queue engine.

**No recommendation is sufficiently supported within the six transmitted cards.** Your confirmed requirements are Python background jobs, scheduling and retries, with Redis, Valkey, RabbitMQ and Kubernetes prohibited. SQLite is available, but the supplied evidence does not establish a compatible SQLite-backed configuration for any of these six repositories. I would leave the adoption decision open rather than choose by retrieval rank.

The frozen catalog is dated September 1, 2026; all six cards have incomplete advisory evidence and `reference_only` eligibility. The host observations dated October 11, 2026 are separate, transient primary-source evidence. In particular, the supplied [Huey observation](https://github.com/coleifer/huey) documents Python tasks, retries, cron, SQLite storage and a separate consumer. That reveals a relevant gap in the transmitted pack, **not an eligible recommendation**: no Huey card was transmitted. The additional IDs in the selection annotations do not expand the six-card boundary.

| Transmitted repository | Assessment for this project |
|---|---|
| [BullMQ](https://github.com/taskforcesh/bullmq) | The frozen description mentions Redis or PostgreSQL, not SQLite. Redis is prohibited; a PostgreSQL configuration would require permission to add that dependency and verification of its Python capabilities, schedules and retries. No supported preference here. |
| [River](https://github.com/riverqueue/river) | The frozen card describes Go background jobs and lists PostgreSQL topics. It does not establish a Python/SQLite path. Adding a Go component and potentially another database would need a demonstrated benefit for your one-engineer project. |
| [Sidekiq](https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq) | The frozen card describes Ruby background processing. It does not establish a compatible backend or a suitable Python integration; dependency and license details remain unresolved in this evidence. |
| [Asynq](https://github.com/hibiken/asynq) | The frozen card describes a Go queue and includes a Redis topic. A topic alone does not prove a mandatory dependency, but the supplied evidence establishes no configuration satisfying your bans. |
| [Trigger.dev](https://github.com/triggerdotdev/trigger.dev) | The frozen description concerns managed workflows, with TypeScript as the primary language. Python integration, deployment dependencies, data handling and provider costs are unverified here. |
| [Temporal Python SDK](https://github.com/temporalio/sdk-python) | Its Python identity is established, but the card does not establish the service requirements, scheduling/retry behavior or an acceptable SQLite deployment. An SDK identity alone does not justify adoption. |

For a subsequently verified compatible component, the proposed architecture would retain your Python API and use this flow: **API → durable job storage → separate worker → application operation**, with scheduled work entering the same execution path. This is a target design, not a capability claim about the six candidates. Whether SQLite holds application data as well as jobs is unknown; do not assume those writes share an atomic transaction.

The technical work would include enqueue integration, job payload/version rules, handlers, schedule definitions, retry limits, worker supervision and failure visibility. The project team would still own authorization, idempotent business effects, the gap between committing application data and enqueueing a job, handling exhausted retries, and rollback. Prefer small identifiers in queued payloads where practical; workers can retrieve authorized application data instead of duplicating sensitive records in job storage.

The expected product benefit is moving suitable work out of request handling and supporting scheduled operations while reusing execution machinery. That could help the engineer concentrate on features, but neither faster delivery nor latency improvement has been measured. Complexity depends especially on persistent storage availability, single-host versus multi-host deployment, SQLite contention, job duration, duplicate-effect consequences, restart recovery and missed-schedule requirements.

**Complete adoption effort is unknown until a compatible component and deployment scope are established.** A bounded first validation can be planned at **4–8 engineer-hours**, assuming one experienced Python engineer, a runnable local API, persistent local storage and one harmless representative job. At six focused engineering hours per engineer-day, that is approximately **0.7–1.3 working days**, allocated entirely to that engineer. Obtaining missing evidence or infrastructure approval is separate external waiting. These are planning estimates, not observed results or commitments.

Compared with equivalent-scope custom development, reuse would still incur integration, upgrades, dependency review and operational maintenance. Custom development would additionally require implementing and maintaining durable job claiming, scheduling, retry state and crash behavior. It could be preferable for unusually narrow requirements, but it conflicts with your stated desire to avoid owning a queue engine. Keeping a current/native solution is reasonable if it already meets the same persistence and failure requirements; its behavior is not supplied, so that comparison remains open. A defensible full effort or savings comparison is unavailable.

**First validation:** request a transmitted card for a Python/SQLite candidate, or establish an acceptable configuration for one of the six before piloting. Then enqueue one job, force a transient failure, run a scheduled occurrence, and interrupt/restart the worker around a business-effect boundary. Inspect durable state, retry exhaustion, duplicate effects and restart behavior; do not assume successful crash recovery. Define the expected behavior before running the check.

The smallest deployment question that changes the next decision is: **Will the API and worker run on one host with persistent SQLite storage, or must jobs execute across multiple hosts?** No tools were used, no integration was performed, and no state or catalog evidence was saved or refreshed.

history.content: Search our own product catalogue with typo tolerance and brand/price filters, not the external web. Typesense remains excluded.

**Evaluate Meilisearch (ID `130688011`) first for your product-search prototype.** Its documented application search, typo tolerance and facets directly address shoppers mistyping product names and narrowing results by brand. The supplied host read dated **2026-10-11** supports this preference, while explicitly leaving indexing, synchronization and relevance validation to your team. Better product discovery is an expected benefit to test, not a measured result. [Meilisearch repository](https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch)

This is a **conditional recommendation for validation**, rather than approval for complete adoption. The supplied evidence does not establish numeric price-range filtering, suitability for your catalog size and languages, hosting compatibility, or the license terms of the exact version you would deploy. In particular, facets alone do not prove that the required price-filter behavior works. Typesense remains excluded.

**Proposed architecture and technical work**

Retain whichever system currently owns your product records and the existing application. Add Meilisearch as a derived search index, with a small JavaScript integration layer:

`Product source → initial export + update/delete synchronization → Meilisearch index`

`Shopper UI → application search endpoint → Meilisearch → product results + filter information`

The application endpoint is a proposed boundary for validating queries and enforcing any visibility rules. Keep indexing/admin credentials on the server. Index only fields shoppers may see; use the authoritative product source to confirm current price and availability when purchasing. This avoids treating a potentially stale search result as transaction authority.

Meilisearch would cover the search-engine role. Your developer would still own the product-document mapping, brand normalization, numeric price representation, synchronization, search UI, relevance tuning and operational checks. The supplied host observation explicitly identifies indexing, synchronization and relevance validation as remaining project work. [Meilisearch repository](https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch)

For shoppers, the proposed outcome is a search box that can recover from common spelling mistakes and allow useful narrowing of results. Whether that actually helps depends on your product names, brands and real query patterns. Semantic search is not established as a requirement, so it should stay outside the first slice.

**Comparison with the other transmitted options and the current solution**

| Option | Assessment for this project | Condition that could change the choice |
|---|---|---|
| **Meilisearch** | Best-supported first validation candidate: the dated host evidence confirms typo tolerance and facets. | Required price filtering, relevance, license or deployment checks fail. |
| **OpenSearch / Elasticsearch** | The frozen cards identify distributed search engines. A broader engine may be appropriate, but these materials do not establish a better fit for this prototype. Mapping, query design and operations would need investigation. | You already operate one, or demonstrate requirements the simpler candidate cannot meet. |
| **Vespa** | The frozen card identifies an AI search platform; the supplied evidence does not resolve the specific typo-tolerance and brand/price workflow. There is no demonstrated reason to introduce that platform scope yet. | A concrete advanced ranking or serving requirement justifies it, and product-search fit is verified. |
| **Crawlee** | Its documented role is crawling and browser automation. Your requirement is search over your own catalog, so it does not supply the required search-engine role. | A separate ingestion need emerges; that would still require a search component. |
| **SereneDB** | The frozen card describes a search analytics database, but the required shopper-search behavior remains unverified. Catalog acceptance does not establish application fit. | A pilot proves the required matching and filters and identifies a relevant architectural advantage. |

These comparisons use the supplied frozen cards, not fresh checks of those alternatives. Sources: [OpenSearch](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch), [Elasticsearch](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch), [Vespa](https://github.com/vespa-engine/vespa), [Crawlee](https://github.com/apify/crawlee), [SereneDB](https://github.com/serenedb/serenedb). They are alternatives or out-of-scope references, not a set to install together.

Keeping your current/native search could be preferable if it already provides acceptable typo recovery and filters. That would avoid another service and synchronization path. Its capabilities are unknown here, so the first validation should compare against it if available. Reuse introduces dependency upgrades, hosting, index recovery and freshness monitoring; custom development introduces ownership of matching, ranking and filter correctness. Reuse does not automatically win.

**Conditional effort estimate**

For planning only, assume one JavaScript developer familiar with the application and HTTP integrations, an accessible product export and update mechanism, at most roughly 10,000 products, one language/currency, public product visibility, and an available deployment environment. Scope is one search UI with typo handling, brand/price filters, synchronization and basic operational recovery. It excludes high availability, personalized pricing, semantic search and a platform migration. Confidence is low to moderate until validation.

| Phase | Meilisearch integration | Equivalent-scope custom search |
|---|---:|---:|
| First validation / baseline and design | 6–10 engineer-hours | 6–10 engineer-hours |
| Matching, ranking and filter implementation | 4–8 | 24–48 |
| Product mapping and update/delete synchronization | 8–16 | 8–16 |
| Application endpoint and search UI | 10–18 | 10–18 |
| Regression checks, recovery and rollout/rollback preparation | 8–14 | 12–24 |
| **Total, including first validation once** | **36–66 engineer-hours** | **60–116 engineer-hours** |

At **8 engineer-hours per engineer-day**, with that developer allocated full time and phases performed sequentially, these scenarios imply **4.5–8.25 working days** for integration and **7.5–14.5 working days** for custom development. The custom estimate means application-specific search over this bounded catalog, not building a general search platform. Neither range is a commitment or measured saving. Hosting procurement, license decisions and owner feedback add unknown waiting time; part-time allocation extends elapsed time. Ongoing maintenance and provider costs are not quantified.

The main complexity drivers are catalog cleanliness, update frequency, multilingual matching, product variants, customer-specific visibility/prices and deployment ownership. If those assumptions do not hold, the complete-adoption total is unknown until scoped. The most useful scope clarification is: **approximately how many products must be searched, and how are product changes available to the application?**

**Concrete first validation**

Use the 6–10-hour slice to index **500–1,000 representative products**, including similar names, inconsistent brand spellings and price-boundary cases. Create **30–50 owner-labeled queries** covering exact names, common typos, ambiguous terms and combined brand/price filters. Compare against current search if available.

Check that intended products appear in the agreed result positions, filters never return out-of-range or wrong-brand items, and a product update and deletion reach the index within an owner-agreed freshness target. Also check the exact deployment version's license, required runtime/client compatibility and credential boundaries. Agree relevance and latency acceptance targets before judging the results; none have been measured here.

Proceed only if that slice demonstrates the required numeric price filtering, useful relevance and an acceptable synchronization/deployment path. Otherwise retain the current component while investigating the failed requirement. The frozen catalog remains unchanged; the supplied 2026-10-11 host observations are transient answer evidence, and no implementation or validation has been executed.
